title: An Elegy for the Landline
script: Narrator: [wry] We disconnected the landline last week, a decision so trivially administrative that I'm faintly embarrassed by how long I mourned it afterward.
Narrator: [reflective] Nobody had dialed that number in years except telemarketers and, twice annually, an aunt who distrusts anything with a screen attached to it.

Narrator: [thoughtful] And yet there was a particular anguish, unearned and entirely disproportionate, to watching the technician disconnect a cord that had, decades ago, delivered every significant piece of news my family ever received.

Narrator: [candid] I keep catching myself romanticizing an object I hadn't consciously thought about in a decade, which tells you less about the telephone than about how selectively nostalgia operates.

Narrator: [wry] It wasn't the ringing I missed, precisely, but the specific vulnerability the ringing implied: you answered without knowing who waited on the other end, an intimacy the caller identification on my phone has quietly, efficiently abolished.
Narrator: [honest] Every call now arrives pre-vetted, filtered through a name and a photograph, stripped of the small, bracing uncertainty that used to precede even the most mundane conversation.

Narrator: [analytical] I suspect what I'm actually grieving isn't the hardware at all but a mode of attention the hardware once enforced: a call demanded your whole, undivided presence, since nothing else was competing for it in that moment.

Narrator: [reflective] My smartphone offers infinitely more, and asks correspondingly less of me, which is either an extraordinary bargain or a slow, imperceptible theft, and I genuinely cannot decide which.
Narrator: [pragmatic] I'm not proposing we resurrect the landline; that would be sentimentality masquerading as principle, and I have little patience for either in myself.

Narrator: [with quiet resolve] But I have started, deliberately, answering calls without first consulting the screen, reintroducing a sliver of that old, bracing uncertainty into a life that has otherwise been thoroughly, comfortably pre-vetted.

quiz.question: What did the narrator's household disconnect last week?
quiz.explanation: The narrator says they disconnected the landline last week.

quiz.question: Who had actually been calling the landline in recent years?
options: Telemarketers and, twice annually, an aunt who distrusts screens
quiz.explanation: He says only telemarketers and an aunt who distrusts screens had called the landline in years.

quiz.question: What does the narrator say he actually misses, more than the ringing itself?
options: The specific vulnerability of answering without knowing who waited on the other end
quiz.explanation: He says he misses the vulnerability implied by not knowing who was calling, not the ringing itself.

quiz.question: How does caller identification affect calls now, according to the narrator?
options: It pre-vets every call, stripping away the small uncertainty that used to precede conversations
It only works for video calls
quiz.explanation: He says caller ID pre-vets calls, removing the bracing uncertainty that once preceded mundane conversations.

quiz.question: What deliberate habit has the narrator started adopting?
options: Answering calls without first consulting the screen
quiz.explanation: He has started deliberately answering calls without first checking the screen, to reintroduce some uncertainty.

title: The Algorithm Knows My Mother Better Than I Do
script: Aisyah: [unsettled] I found my mother's phone open to an advertisement so precisely tailored to her situation that I genuinely wondered, briefly, whether someone had been listening to our private conversations.
Rendra: [wry] Nobody needed to listen. The inference alone is damning enough without invoking anything so dramatic as surveillance.
Aisyah: [curious] Meaning what, exactly? She hasn't searched for anything remotely related.

Rendra: [explanatory] She didn't need to. Enough adjacent behavior, browsing patterns, the time she lingers on certain articles, the pauses before she scrolls past something, aggregates into a portrait more candid than most confessions.
Aisyah: [troubled] That's a considerably more intimate portrait than I'd feel comfortable handing a stranger, and yet she's handed it over without ever consciously agreeing to anything.
Rendra: [measured] Consent, in this context, is largely theatrical. Nobody reads the document; everybody clicks accept, and the theater satisfies a legal requirement rather than an ethical one.
Aisyah: [frustrated] So what would meaningful consent even look like, practically, for someone her age who barely trusts the device to begin with?

Rendra: [thoughtful] Probably something closer to a standing conversation than a one-time checkbox, revisited periodically as her circumstances shift, rather than buried in a document nobody was ever expected to read.
Aisyah: [skeptical] That sounds appealing in theory and entirely unprofitable in practice, which is presumably why no platform has volunteered for it.
Rendra: [dry] Precisely. The business model depends on exactly the opacity you're objecting to. Transparency and profitability are, in this particular arrangement, natural adversaries.
Aisyah: [resolute] Then I suppose the least I can do is sit with her and actually walk through what she's agreed to, badly translated legalese and all.
Rendra: [warmly] That's not nothing. An hour of genuine explanation probably does more good than any regulation currently pending.
Aisyah: [wry] Small comfort, given how thoroughly the algorithm's already finished its portrait of her.
Rendra: [gently] Finished portraits can still be corrected, Aisyah. That's rather the whole point of intervening now instead of never.

quiz.question: What did Aisyah find on her mother's phone?
options: An advertisement so precisely tailored it seemed like someone had been listening in
quiz.explanation: Aisyah found an advertisement so precisely tailored that she wondered if someone had been listening to their conversations.

quiz.question: According to Rendra, how is such precise targeting achieved without direct searches?
options: Through aggregating adjacent behavior like browsing patterns and pauses before scrolling
quiz.explanation: Rendra explains that adjacent behavior aggregates into a detailed portrait without any direct search being needed.

quiz.question: How does Rendra describe consent in this context?
options: Largely theatrical, satisfying a legal requirement rather than an ethical one
quiz.explanation: Rendra says consent is largely theatrical, satisfying legal rather than ethical requirements.

quiz.question: What does Rendra say the business model depends on?
options: The exact opacity that Aisyah objects to
quiz.explanation: Rendra says the business model depends on the opacity Aisyah is objecting to, making transparency and profit adversaries.

quiz.question: What does Aisyah decide to do by the end of the conversation?
options: Sit with her mother and walk through what she has agreed to
quiz.explanation: Aisyah resolves to sit with her mother and actually walk through what she's agreed to, badly translated legalese included.

title: On the Discipline of Being Findable
script: Narrator: [wry] There is a particular exhaustion, rarely named precisely, that comes not from working too much but from being perpetually available to work, which turns out to be an entirely different affliction.

Narrator: [analytical] I used to conflate the two, assuming that if I merely reduced my hours, the exhaustion would recede proportionally, and it never quite did, which puzzled me for longer than I'd like to admit.

Narrator: [reflective] What finally clarified things was noticing that my shoulders tensed the instant I glimpsed a notification, regardless of whether I opened it, regardless even of whether I was technically off duty at the time.
Narrator: [candid] The mere possibility of a demand, it turns out, exacts nearly the same toll as the demand itself, a discovery that felt less like insight than accusation.

Narrator: [thoughtful] We've built, almost accidentally, an economy that prizes findability as though it were a virtue indistinguishable from diligence, when in fact they share almost nothing beyond a superficial resemblance.
Narrator: [firm] Diligence is what you do with your attention once it's engaged. Findability is merely surrendering the right to decide when it gets engaged at all.

Narrator: [honest] I spent years mistaking the second for the first, priding myself on rapid replies at inconvenient hours as though responsiveness were itself an achievement rather than simply an erosion I'd stopped noticing.

Narrator: [determined] So I've instituted something almost comically modest: a window, roughly ninety minutes each evening, during which the phone is physically elsewhere, out of both reach and eyeline.
Narrator: [wry] The withdrawal, I confess, was considerably more acute than I'd anticipated for something this small, which itself told me everything about how deep the habit had rooted.

Narrator: [warmly] Ninety minutes is a modest ambition, I realize, hardly the stuff of a manifesto. But it's the first ninety minutes in years during which nobody, anywhere, could summon my attention without my prior consent.

quiz.question: What kind of exhaustion does the narrator distinguish from simply working too much?
options: The exhaustion of being perpetually available to work
quiz.explanation: She distinguishes exhaustion from overwork from the distinct exhaustion of being perpetually available.

quiz.question: What did the narrator notice about her body when she glimpsed a notification?
options: Her shoulders tensed, regardless of whether she opened it or was off duty
quiz.explanation: She noticed her shoulders tensed at the mere sight of a notification, regardless of opening it or being off duty.

quiz.question: How does the narrator distinguish diligence from findability?
options: They are essentially the same thing
Diligence is what you do with engaged attention; findability is surrendering the right to decide when it engages
Findability is more valuable than diligence
quiz.explanation: She defines diligence as directing engaged attention, while findability surrenders the right to decide when attention engages at all.

quiz.question: What modest habit has the narrator instituted?
options: A roughly ninety-minute window each evening when her phone is physically out of reach
Turning off her phone for a full week
quiz.explanation: She has instituted a roughly ninety-minute evening window during which her phone is physically elsewhere.

quiz.question: What did the intensity of her withdrawal reveal to the narrator?
options: That the habit was shallow and easy to break
How deeply the habit of constant availability had rooted
That she should abandon the experiment
That ninety minutes was too short to matter
quiz.explanation: The unexpectedly acute withdrawal revealed to her how deeply the habit of findability had rooted.

title: Two Engineers Argue About Whether They Made Anything Beautiful
script: Galih: [uneasy] Six years building this recommendation engine, and I've started wondering whether we've built anything I'd actually defend on its merits, or merely something that works.
Prita: [pointed] Those aren't mutually exclusive, Galih. Plenty of things work brilliantly while being, in some larger sense, indefensible.
Galih: [candid] That's rather my worry, precisely. It optimizes for engagement with a ruthlessness I find difficult to admire, even as I remain professionally proud of the elegance underneath it.

Prita: [thoughtful] I've made peace with that particular tension, mostly by separating the craft from the deployment. The engineering can be beautiful even when its application is, at minimum, ethically ambiguous.
Galih: [challenging] Can it, though? Or is that distinction just a convenient partition we've built to protect our own conscience from the thing we're actually paid to optimize?

Prita: [conceding] Possibly. I won't pretend the partition is airtight. But the alternative, refusing any craft whose downstream use might be questionable, would rule out nearly every consequential piece of engineering ever built.
Galih: [considering] Fair, and yet there's a meaningful difference between unpredictable downstream misuse and an outcome we deliberately engineered toward from the outset.

Prita: [firm] Agreed, and that distinction is exactly where I think our actual responsibility sits, not in refusing the work, but in refusing to look away from what we've deliberately optimized it to do.
Galih: [honest] I haven't been looking away, if I'm honest. I've been looking directly at it and simply telling myself the elegance excuses the target.
Prita: [gently] That's a harder confession than most engineers manage. Most of us prefer the comfortable fiction that neutrality is even available to us.
Galih: [resolved] I don't think it is, not anymore. I think I'd rather build something less impressive that I could actually stand behind without flinching.
Prita: [warmly] Then propose it. I'd rather argue with you about a worse metric and a clearer conscience than keep perfecting a machine neither of us can fully defend.

quiz.question: What has Galih started wondering after six years on the recommendation engine?
options: Whether they've built anything he'd actually defend on its merits, beyond it simply working
Whether Prita is a good colleague
quiz.explanation: Galih wonders whether they've built something defensible on its merits, not merely something functional.

quiz.question: How does Prita initially try to reconcile the tension Galih raises?
options: By separating the craft from the deployment, seeing engineering as beautiful even when its application is ambiguous
quiz.explanation: Prita separates the elegance of the craft from the ethics of its deployment as her initial coping strategy.

quiz.question: What distinction does Galih draw regarding downstream effects?
options: There is no meaningful distinction to draw
A difference between unpredictable misuse and an outcome deliberately engineered toward from the outset
All outcomes are equally the engineers' fault
quiz.explanation: Galih distinguishes between unpredictable downstream misuse and a deliberately engineered outcome.

quiz.question: What confession does Galih make about his own behavior?
options: That he has been ignoring the ethical questions entirely
That he has been looking directly at the issue and telling himself the elegance excuses the target
That he never noticed any ethical tension
That he wants to blame Prita
quiz.explanation: Galih admits he has been looking directly at the problem while telling himself elegance excuses the target.

quiz.question: What does Galih ultimately decide he would rather build?
options: Nothing at all, leaving the field
Something less impressive that he could actually stand behind without flinching
A system identical to the current one
quiz.explanation: Galih resolves he would rather build something less impressive that he could stand behind without flinching.

title: The Grandmother Who Outsmarted the Scam
script: Dimas: [amazed] Oma, you're telling me you strung the scammer along for twenty minutes before hanging up, purely for your own entertainment?
Oma Ratih: [wry] Purely for entertainment, and partly out of a lifelong grudge against people who assume old age is synonymous with credulity.
Dimas: [curious] What tipped you off in the first place? They're usually quite convincing these days.

Oma Ratih: [dry] The manufactured urgency, mostly. Genuine institutions rarely demand you resolve an emergency within the next ninety seconds while conveniently refusing to let you call back on a number you'd verify yourself.
Dimas: [impressed] That's sharper instinct than half my colleagues have, and they build software for a living.
Oma Ratih: [amused] Instinct built on decades of being underestimated has its uses, apparently. Once he realized I wasn't panicking on schedule, his script started fraying rather badly.
Dimas: [curious] Did he ever catch on that you were toying with him?
Oma Ratih: [smiling] Eventually, yes, and rather abruptly, once I asked him to spell his supposed employer's name and he stumbled over it in a way no legitimate representative ever would.
Dimas: [thoughtful] I worry more about your neighbor, honestly, the one who isn't quite as suspicious of unfamiliar callers as you are.
Oma Ratih: [serious] So do I, which is precisely why I've started sharing these stories at the community gathering rather than keeping them as private amusement.
Dimas: [warmly] That's a better use of the story than I'd given you credit for. I assumed it was purely for the satisfaction of outwitting him.
Oma Ratih: [dry] It was that too. I contain multitudes, Dimas, including a petty streak I've stopped apologizing for at my age.
Dimas: [laughing] Fair enough. Just promise me you'll actually hang up next time rather than negotiating for sport.
Oma Ratih: [firm] I promise nothing of the sort. A woman needs her hobbies.

quiz.question: How long did Oma Ratih string the scammer along?
quiz.explanation: Oma Ratih kept the scammer on the phone for twenty minutes before hanging up.

quiz.question: What tipped Oma Ratih off that the call was a scam?
options: The manufactured urgency and refusal to let her call back on a verifiable number
A misspelled name in a text
quiz.explanation: She says the manufactured urgency and refusal to allow a callback on a verified number tipped her off.

quiz.question: What eventually made the scammer's script fall apart, according to Oma Ratih?
options: She threatened to call the police
He realized she wasn't panicking on schedule and stumbled spelling his employer's name
Her grandson took over the call
quiz.explanation: The script frayed once she wasn't panicking on schedule, and he stumbled spelling his supposed employer's name.

quiz.question: What has Oma Ratih started doing with these scam stories?
options: Sharing them at the community gathering to warn less suspicious neighbors
Reporting them only to the police
quiz.explanation: She has started sharing the stories at the community gathering, especially concerned about a less suspicious neighbor.

quiz.question: Does Oma Ratih promise to simply hang up next time instead of engaging scammers?
options: No, she refuses, saying a woman needs her hobbies
She says she'll think about it
quiz.explanation: She firmly refuses to promise that, saying a woman needs her hobbies.

title: The Cartographer of My Own Attention
script: Narrator: [reflective] I began, somewhat obsessively, tracking every app I opened for a month, less out of discipline than a nagging suspicion that my own account of my days had grown quietly unreliable.
Narrator: [wry] The suspicion, it turns out, was generous to myself; the actual figures were considerably more damning than anything I'd braced for.
Narrator: [candid] I had estimated perhaps ninety minutes daily surrendered to idle scrolling, a figure I'd already considered mildly embarrassing, and the true number nearly tripled it.

Narrator: [thoughtful] What unsettled me wasn't merely the volume but the total absence of memory attached to it, entire evenings that had simply evaporated without leaving behind a single retrievable image or thought.

Narrator: [analytical] Compare that to an hour spent reading, which I can usually reconstruct in some detail weeks later, and you begin to suspect that not all hours are created equal, however identically the clock renders them.
Narrator: [reflective] Some hours accumulate, becoming part of the architecture of a person; others simply pass through, leaving no more residue than water through an open hand.

Narrator: [honest] I don't say this as an indictment of the platforms alone, tempting as that convenient villain remains; I chose, each time, to open the application, however thoroughly its design conspired against my closing it again.
Narrator: [determined] So I've become, rather grandly, the cartographer of my own attention, mapping where it actually travels rather than where I'd like to believe it goes.
Narrator: [wry] The map is unflattering, as most honest maps of the self tend to be, but at least it's now accurate, which strikes me as the necessary precondition for revising the territory at all.

Narrator: [warmly] I haven't reclaimed all those evaporated hours, and perhaps I never fully will. But I notice the vanishing now, in real time, which is a considerably more modest achievement than reform, and a considerably more honest one.

quiz.question: Why did the narrator begin tracking every app he opened for a month?
options: A nagging suspicion that his own account of his days had grown unreliable
He wanted to sell the data
quiz.explanation: He began tracking out of a nagging suspicion that his account of his days had become unreliable.

quiz.question: How did the actual figures compare to the narrator's estimate?
options: The true number nearly tripled his estimate of ninety minutes daily
The true number was lower than expected
quiz.explanation: He had estimated ninety minutes daily, but the true figure nearly tripled that estimate.

quiz.question: What unsettled the narrator most about the scrolling time?
options: The cost of his phone plan
The total absence of memory attached to it, with entire evenings evaporating
That his friends knew about it
The battery drain on his phone
quiz.explanation: He was most unsettled by the complete absence of retrievable memory from those scrolling hours.

quiz.question: What comparison does the narrator draw with reading?
options: Reading and scrolling produce identical memories
An hour of reading can usually be reconstructed in detail weeks later, unlike scrolling
Reading takes more time than scrolling
quiz.explanation: He contrasts scrolling with reading, which he can often reconstruct in detail weeks later.

quiz.question: What does the narrator call himself after starting this tracking practice?
options: The cartographer of his own attention
quiz.explanation: He describes himself as having become the cartographer of his own attention, mapping where it actually travels.

title: Teaching My Father to Distrust His Feed
script: Father: [defensive] I don't need a tutorial, Yasmin. I've read that article three times, and it's clearly well-researched.
Yasmin: [gentle] Can I ask what made it feel well-researched to you, specifically?
Father: [confident] It cited numbers, it sounded confident, and frankly it confirmed what I already suspected was true.
Yasmin: [careful] That last part concerns me more than the first two, honestly. Confirming a prior suspicion is a reason to read something more skeptically, not less.
Father: [defensive] You're suggesting I only believe things that flatter my existing opinions. That's rather insulting, coming from my own daughter.
Yasmin: [firm] I'm suggesting all of us do that, myself included, and the feed knows it better than we do, which is precisely why it keeps surfacing exactly this kind of article for you.
Father: [skeptical] So the algorithm is choosing my beliefs now? That sounds like the conspiracy theory, not the article.
Yasmin: [patient] Not choosing them from nothing, no, but amplifying whichever ones already generate your attention, and attention is the entire currency it's optimizing for.
Father: [considering] Alright, hypothetically, humor me. How would I even tell a well-researched article from a convincing one?
Yasmin: [encouraging] Start by checking whether the same claim, in roughly the same words, appears anywhere outside sources that already agree with each other.
Father: [trying] And if it doesn't?
Yasmin: [gently] Then it's probably one voice amplified into an echo, which sounds like a chorus but is really just a single opinion bouncing off itself.
Father: [reluctant] I suppose I have occasionally mistaken volume for consensus.
Yasmin: [warmly] We all have, Dad. I'm not trying to make you paranoid, just slightly slower to nod along before checking.
Father: [wry] Slower to nod along. At my age, that's practically a personality transplant.
Yasmin: [laughing] I'll settle for a slight renovation. The transplant can wait for next year.

quiz.question: Why did the father initially find the article well-researched?
options: It cited numbers, sounded confident, and confirmed what he already suspected
It was published by a university
quiz.explanation: The father says it cited numbers, sounded confident, and confirmed his existing suspicions.

quiz.question: Why does Yasmin say confirming a prior suspicion should prompt more skepticism?
options: Because it's a reason to read something more skeptically, not less, since we all favor flattering opinions
Because confirmed suspicions are always false
Because it means the source is paid
quiz.explanation: Yasmin explains that confirming a prior suspicion is a reason for more skepticism, not less, since everyone favors flattering information.

quiz.question: What does Yasmin say the algorithm optimizes for?
options: Attention, amplifying whichever beliefs already generate engagement
quiz.explanation: Yasmin says attention is the entire currency the algorithm optimizes for, amplifying beliefs that generate it.

quiz.question: What test does Yasmin suggest for checking a claim?
options: Checking the number of likes it received
Checking whether the same claim appears outside sources that already agree with each other
Asking a friend for their opinion
quiz.explanation: Yasmin suggests checking whether the claim appears outside sources that already agree with each other.

quiz.question: What does the father admit by the end of the conversation?
options: That the article was completely false
That he has occasionally mistaken volume for consensus
That he will stop using the internet
That Yasmin is wrong about everything
quiz.explanation: The father admits he has occasionally mistaken volume for consensus.
